clips.title: The Human Is an Async API — Melanie Warrick, Temporal
clips.why: A short framing of the problem this lesson solves: a person answers in hours or days, so an agent must wait for them without holding anything.
look: "The human is an async API": you call it and the answer comes back much later.
Her list of what belongs in a harness, and where durability fits.
Notice that waiting is treated as a normal step, not an error.
clips.after: ticketToPr waits for the plan decision with a durable timer, and holds no VM and no slot while the requester thinks.

clips.title: Bulkhead Pattern Explained: Resilience in Microservices Architecture
clips.why: The bulkhead pattern gives each kind of work its own fixed pool, so a flood of one kind of work cannot take what the others need, which is what our slots and queues do per agent.
look: The ship picture: a leak fills one compartment, not the whole ship.
A thread pool per service is a fixed number of seats, like Nova's 3 slots.
When the pool is full, new work waits instead of taking resources from others.
clips.after: Our compartments are agents: Nova has 3 VM slots and its own queue, so a storm of Nova tickets cannot take the CI fixer's machines.

clips.title: The Bulkhead Pattern: How To Make Your System Fault-tolerant
clips.why: A second, more hands-on view: the problem of one consumer using up a shared resource, and how isolation fixes it.
look: In the problem part, watch what happens to everything else when one consumer holds a shared resource for too long.
Isolation means separate limits for separate work, not one big shared limit.
Compare his separate pools with our separate task queues and slot lines.
clips.after: In our platform a slow approval would be that slow consumer, which is why a run gives its slot back while it waits for a person.

practice.q: Put one sandbox step of ticketToPr in order.
items: workInSandbox runs the harness and heartbeats
finally: releaseSandbox, in a non-cancellable scope
practice.why: The slot is taken before the VM and given back after it, so the number of running VMs can never be higher than the number of slots.

practice.q: Make the VM release run even when the workflow is cancelled.
practice.hint: A scope that cannot be cancelled.
practice.why: A cancelled workflow cancels its own activity calls too. Inside nonCancellable the release still runs, so no VM is left behind.

practice.q: Three runs are waiting for plan approval when the orchestrator is deployed and its workers restart. What happens to the waits?

options.text: Nothing changes: each wait is a durable timer in Temporal, and the new workers continue it
options.why: Temporal stores the timer and the run's history, not the worker. A new worker replays the history, and the wait continues with the time that has already passed.

options.text: The waits start again from zero, so the reminders come a day later
options.why: The timer lives in Temporal with its start time, so a restart neither resets it nor makes it longer.

options.text: The runs fail, and the Jira poll starts them again a minute later
options.why: Nothing fails. A worker restart is normal, and Temporal gives the runs to the new workers.

practice.q: Which timeout tells Temporal that the worker running workInSandbox has died?

options.why: That one is only a far safety net, and when it fires the retry re-attaches to the same harness.
A live activity heartbeats every few seconds; two minutes of silence means the process is gone.
We set no run timeout. A run ends when its work ends, or when a person stops it.

practice.q: Finish the line that decides when slots:nova may hand out the next slot.
practice.hint: How many runs hold a slot right now.
practice.why: The line grants a slot only when someone is waiting and fewer runs hold a slot than the agent's number, so Nova never has more than three VMs at once.
